title: Elastic Potential Energy
short: A spring stretched or squeezed by x stores ½kx².
trouble: Students write kx² without the ½, or use the force kx as if it were energy.

blocks.html: A stretched spring can launch a toy or start a clock, so it stores energy. How much? It equals the work done to deform it, which is the area under the force-stretch graph.

A spring stretched or compressed by $x$ from its natural length stores elastic potential energy $\role[spring potential energy]{energy}{U_s} = \tfrac12 \role[spring constant]{constant}{k}\role[stretch or compression]{position}{x}^2$.

The force needed grows from $0$ to $kx$ as you stretch the spring (Hooke's law), so the $F$–$x$ graph is a straight line through the origin. The work is the triangle under it: $\tfrac12 \times x \times kx = \tfrac12 kx^2$. The $\tfrac12$ comes from the triangle; the square comes from the force and the distance both growing with $x$.

opts.task: Double the stretch from 0.1 m to 0.2 m. How does the area change?

blocks.cap: k = 400 N/m: at 0.1 m the triangle is 2 J; at 0.2 m it is 8 J, four times as much.

blocks.title: Energy stored
blocks.q: A spring with $k = 250\ \text{N/m}$ is compressed $12\ \text{cm}$. How much energy does it store?

blocks.title: Stretch from energy
blocks.q: How far must a spring with $k = 500\ \text{N/m}$ be stretched to store $4\ \text{J}$?

blocks.title: Adding stretch
blocks.q: A spring with $k = 300\ \text{N/m}$ is already stretched $5\ \text{cm}$. How much more energy does it take to stretch it to $10\ \text{cm}$?
steps: Not $\tfrac12(300)(0.05)^2 = 0.375\ \text{J}$: the second $5\ \text{cm}$ is harder than the first.

blocks.html: Because the energy grows as $x^2$, the last few centimeters of a stretch store the most energy: going from $0.1$ to $0.2\ \text{m}$ above adds $6\ \text{J}$, three times as much as the first $0.1\ \text{m}$.

Writing $kx^2$ without the $\tfrac12$, or using the force $kx$ as if it were the energy. Check the units: $kx$ is in N, a force; $\tfrac12 kx^2$ is in N·m = J, an energy. And doubling the stretch should multiply the energy by four, not two.
